documents.source: Preamble and Declaration of Principles of the Knights of Labor (1878). Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The Knights’ own statement of aims; shows how broad the first national union’s goals were.
documents.text: “To secure to the toilers a proper share of the wealth that they create; more of the leisure that rightfully belongs to them. . . . The prohibition of the employment of children in workshops, mines, and factories before attaining their fourteenth year. . . . To secure for both sexes equal pay for equal work. The reduction of the hours of labor to eight per day.”
documents.title: The Knights of Labor state their aims

documents.source: August Spies, address to the court, October 7, 1886, in The Chicago Martyrs (1899). Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A condemned anarchist speaking in his own defense; shows how labor radicals framed the trial.
documents.text: “There was not a syllable said about Anarchism at the Haymarket meeting. At that meeting the very popular theme of reducing the hours of toil was discussed. . . . You may pronounce the sentence upon me, honorable judge, but let the world know that in A.D. 1886, in the State of Illinois, eight men were sentenced to death, because they believed in a better future.”
documents.title: Spies on the Haymarket meeting

documents.source: Samuel Gompers, address to the International Labor Congress, August 28, 1893. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The AFL president’s own words; shows labor’s demands reaching past wages.
documents.text: “What does labor want? It wants the earth and the fullness thereof. . . . We want more schoolhouses and less jails; more books and less arsenals; more learning and less vice; . . . more leisure and less greed; more justice and less revenge; in fact, more of the opportunities to cultivate our better natures. . . .”
documents.title: Gompers on what labor wants

documents.source: Historical Statistics of the United States, Table Ba4954-4964 (work stoppages, workers involved). Public data.
documents.sourcing: Government strike counts; shows how fast labor conflict grew in the 1880s.
documents.title: Work stoppages and workers involved

documents.source: “Promise and Performance” political cartoon on the Homestead strike, 1892. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A cartoonist’s view of Homestead; shows how the public saw Carnegie’s wealth against locked-out workers.
documents.title: A cartoon of Homestead

documents.source: In re Debs, 158 U.S. 564 (1895). Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The Supreme Court’s own words; shows the nation’s power used against a strike.
documents.text: “The entire strength of the nation may be used to enforce in any part of the land the full and free exercise of all national powers and the security of all rights entrusted by the Constitution to its care.”
documents.title: The Supreme Court on the nation’s strength

documents.source: Harper’s Weekly engraving of the Haymarket Square bombing, May 15, 1886. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A news engraving from the week of the bombing; shows how readers pictured the violence.
documents.title: The Haymarket bombing

books.section: Topic 6.7 Labor in the Gilded Age

primary_sources: Preamble and Declaration of Principles of the Knights of Labor (1878)
August Spies, address to the court (October 7, 1886)
Samuel Gompers, address to the International Labor Congress (August 28, 1893)
Historical Statistics of the United States, Table Ba4954-4964
“Promise and Performance” political cartoon on the Homestead strike (1892)
Harper’s Weekly engraving of the Haymarket Square bombing (May 15, 1886)

modelOutline:
Thesis: Between 1865 and 1898 organized labor changed American society deeply but unevenly, building national unions, forcing the eight-hour day and child-labor reform onto the public agenda, and teaching workers to act together, while losing nearly every great strike and leaving the balance of power with employers and the courts.
Context: The Civil War ended with factories, railroads, and mines growing fast, and with immigrants, women, and children flooding into industrial work for low pay and long hours.
Evidence: Documents 1 and 3 show the unions’ programs: the Knights demand a share of the wealth workers create, an end to child labor, equal pay, and the eight-hour day, while Gompers asks for schools, books, leisure, and justice. Document 4 shows the movement’s scale: stoppages tripled and workers involved nearly quadrupled between 1884 and 1886.
Evidence continued: Documents 5 and 7 show the public face of the struggle: a cartoon of Carnegie on money bags above locked-out workers, and an engraving of the Haymarket bomb blast. Documents 2 and 6 show the cost: Spies sentenced to death for believing in a better future, and the Supreme Court placing the entire strength of the nation behind the strike’s defeat.
Outside evidence: The Great Railroad Strike of 1877 brought federal troops against strikers, the Homestead lockout of 1892 ended with 8,000 National Guard troops retaking the mill, and the AFL kept growing after 1886 while the Knights faded.
Complexity: the same movement that gave workers a voice and a program also frightened the public and the courts, so labor changed what Americans argued about even where it lost the strike itself.
prompt: Evaluate the extent to which organized labor changed American society between 1865 and 1898.

rubric.criterion: Earns the point for a thesis that makes a historically defensible claim about the extent to which organized labor changed American society between 1865 and 1898, with a line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: A thesis that merely restates the prompt, or one that makes no claim about extent, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as post-Civil War industrialization, the growth of corporations, or the rise of national unions.
rubric.notEarned: A context that is only background on one document, or one set outside the period, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Earns the point for using the content of at least three documents to support the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than three documents, or quoting documents without connecting them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Earns the point for using at least six documents to support the argument, with specific evidence from each.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or listing documents without using their content, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Earns the point for using at least one piece of specific outside evidence, such as the Great Railroad Strike of 1877, the Homestead lockout, or the AFL’s growth after 1886, to support the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Repeating document content without adding outside evidence does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Earns the point for explaining how at least one document’s point of view, purpose, historical situation, or audience matters to the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Identifying a document’s author without explaining why that matters does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Earns the point for a complex argument, such as showing that labor changed some parts of American life while leaving others unchanged, or that the same changes helped some Americans and hurt others.
rubric.notEarned: A one-sided argument that ignores counter-evidence, or a complexity move stated without support, does not earn the point.
